---
title: "Methods: sorting motifs by subject"
description: "How the Sjónabók gallery groups patterns by what they depict (birds, flowers, deer and more): a practical guide to using AI to sort a collection, with a person making every decision."
---

Many Sjónabók patterns depict something: a bird, a flower in a vase, a reindeer, a heart, a
human figure. This page explains how we group them by subject, step by step, so that anyone can
check the result or repeat the method on their own collection. Every script, setting and label is
in the [Sjonabok repository](https://github.com/HiDefTextiles/Sjonabok/tree/main/analysis/subjects).

::: {.heimild}
**The rule we follow: the computer proposes, a person decides.** No subject shown in the gallery
was set by a computer. AI is used to put similar charts next to each other so that a person can
label them quickly and consistently. Every label carries the name of the person who set it and
the date.
:::

## Why not let the AI decide?

Image models are trained mostly on photographs. A Sjónabók chart is different: a bird may be
10 × 10 cells of black and white, drawn in a style several centuries old. A model can tell that
two charts *look alike*, and that is useful, but it cannot be trusted to say that a chart *is a
bird*. A wrong label in a public gallery is worse than no label. So the AI does the tedious part,
sorting 600 charts into small piles of look-alikes, and a person does the part that needs
knowledge.

## The workflow at a glance

| Step | Done by | What happens | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Units | Computer | Pick what to compare: a whole motif, or one repeat of a band | `units.csv` |
| 2. Shape distance | Computer | Compare every pair of charts cell by cell, ignoring flips, turns and shifts | `shape_dist.csv` |
| 3. Image model | Computer | Describe each chart with a pretrained image model and compare the descriptions | `embed_dist.csv` |
| 4. Clusters | Computer | Put the charts into about 50 small piles of look-alikes | `clusters.csv` |
| 5. Review | Person | Look at each pile, name its subject, pick out the odd ones | `review.csv` → `subjects.csv` |
| 6. Suggestions | Computer | For charts not yet reviewed, suggest the subject of their nearest labelled neighbours | `suggestions.csv` |
| 7. Gallery | Computer | Show reviewed subjects as a filter | the *Subject* filter |

Steps 1 to 4 and 6 can be rerun at any time and give the same result. Step 5 is the only one
whose output is written by a person, and a rerun never changes it.

## Step 1: what is compared {#units}

A stand-alone motif or rosette is compared as the whole chart, with its empty margin trimmed.
A border band repeats one figure many times, so it is compared on one repeat (the
[repeat unit](about.qmd#repeats)), otherwise a band of six birds would look nothing like a single
bird. The first round, the *pilot*, covers the 233 motifs and rosettes. Bands follow once the
pilot has been reviewed.

## Step 2: shape distance {#shape}

Each chart is shrunk to a 16 × 16 grey picture and compared with every other chart in all eight
turned and mirrored positions. The best match counts (a correlation between the pictures), and
the distance is one minus that match. This is the same comparison as
[similar patterns](about.qmd#similar). It is exact and easy to explain, and it is good at finding
copies and close variants of the same figure. It is poor at meaning: a bird with raised wings and
one with lowered wings can be far apart.

## Step 3: a pretrained image model {#embedding}

An *image model* is a neural network that has already learnt, from millions of pictures, to
describe an image as a list of numbers (an *embedding*). Pictures that look alike to people get
similar lists. We use [DINOv2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07193), an openly published model, in
its smallest size (ViT-S/14, loaded with the `timm` library from Hugging Face), which describes each picture with 384 numbers and runs on an
ordinary laptop without a graphics card. We do not train or change the model.

For each chart we:

1. draw it black on white in a 224 × 224 square, enlarging whole cells so the edges stay sharp;
2. do this in all eight turned and mirrored positions and average the eight descriptions, so a
   bird facing left and one facing right are described the same way;
3. compare two charts by the angle between their descriptions (one minus the cosine similarity).

The model sees the overall form, a beak and legs, a stem with leaves, better than the cell-by-cell
comparison does. It can also be fooled by texture or by how dense a chart is, which is why its
result is only a proposal.

## Step 4: clusters {#clusters}

The charts are grouped by the image-model distance from step 3. We also tried averaging it with
the shape distance from step 2 (each first turned into ranks between 0 and 1 so they share a
scale). On the pilot that mixed deer, stars and flowers in the same piles, while the image model
alone kept the animals together, so the shape distance now gets weight 0. It is kept in the
code, because it is used when the image model cannot be run and it may help other collections.
The charts are then grouped with
[hierarchical clustering](https://search.r-project.org/R/refmans/stats/html/hclust.html)
in R (Ward's method). This builds a family tree of the charts, joining the most alike first,
and the tree is cut into 50 piles.

Fifty is deliberately more than the number of subjects. Small, pure piles are quick to review;
large piles mix subjects and have to be sorted chart by chart. Two piles of birds are no problem,
they get the same label. The piles are numbered along the tree, so neighbouring numbers look alike.

We first tried *average linkage*. It joined most charts into one pile of 55 and left many piles
of one, so we changed to Ward's method, which keeps piles of similar size (largest 18 in the pilot).

## Step 5: the review {#review}

The reviewer opens a review page that works on a phone: one card per pile, with every chart drawn
from its 0/1 file. For each pile they tap:

- **subject**: one word from the [subject list](https://github.com/HiDefTextiles/Sjonabok/blob/main/analysis/subjects/vocabulary.csv)
  (bird, flower, tree, deer, other animal, human figure, heart, star, cross, letters, geometric,
  not sure). A chart can have several subjects, for example a bird on a flowering branch.
- **exceptions**: tap a chart that does not fit to see it large and give it its own subject.
- **mixed**: if the pile is too varied, it is left for a finer cut in the next round.

The answers are exported as `review.csv`, one row per pile. The page is in the repository
(`analysis/subjects/review/`, started with `make review`), so the next round, or another collection,
can be reviewed the same way. In our pilot one person reviewed 34 piles in about eight minutes.

`make labels` then writes one row per chart into `subjects.csv`: the chart, its subjects, the
reviewer's name, the date and any note. This file is the result of the whole method, and it is the
only file a person writes.

## Step 6: suggestions for the rest {#suggestions}

Once some charts are labelled, each unlabelled chart gets a suggestion: the most common subject
among its five nearest labelled charts, with how many of the five agree. Suggestions go into the
next review round to speed it up. They are never shown in the gallery as a subject.

## Step 7: the gallery {#gallery}

When the gallery is built, `subjects.csv` is read and each pattern gets its reviewed subjects.
They appear as the *Subject* filter and in the pattern view. Charts not yet reviewed are listed
as *Not yet sorted*.

## Open and repeatable {#reproducible}

- **Code and settings are public.** All steps are in
  [`analysis/subjects/`](https://github.com/HiDefTextiles/Sjonabok/tree/main/analysis/subjects):
  `subjects.py` (steps 1, 2, 5, 6), `embed.py` (step 3) and `cluster.R` (step 4), run in order
  by a `Makefile`.
- **The same input gives the same output.** Clustering has no random element; the image model
  runs on the processor in PyTorch's deterministic mode; the model name and a fingerprint (SHA-256)
  of its weights are recorded with each run.
- **Only human work is stored.** Distances, piles and contact sheets are rebuilt from the charts
  in minutes, so they are not kept in git. `review.csv` and `subjects.csv` are kept, with names
  and dates, and every change to them is visible in the repository history.
- **Labels belong to charts, not piles.** Pile numbers change between runs; labels are stored by
  the chart's file name, so a new run cannot move or lose them.

## Try it on your own collection {#guide}

The method works for any set of small images: other pattern books, stamps, logos, fossils. What
you need: Python 3 with NumPy and Pillow, R with the tidyverse, and for step 3 PyTorch and timm
(`pip install torch timm`; the model, about 85 MB, downloads itself the first time).

```bash
git clone https://github.com/HiDefTextiles/Sjonabok
cd Sjonabok/analysis/subjects
make embed                # steps 1 and 3: units and the image model
make                      # steps 2 and 4 and the contact sheets
make review               # step 5: review on a phone or laptop, export review.csv
make labels REVIEWER="Your Name"
make suggest              # suggestions for the next round
```

Lessons from our pilot that carry over:

1. **Start small.** Run the whole loop on a few hundred items before scaling up. Our pilot is the
   233 motifs and rosettes.
2. **Over-split on purpose.** Many small piles are faster to label than a few large mixed ones.
3. **Label piles, fix exceptions.** Naming a pile of 12 birds is one decision, not twelve.
4. **Keep a fixed vocabulary.** Decide the subject words before reviewing, and add a word only on
   purpose, so labels stay consistent between people and rounds.
5. **Keep people's decisions as data.** Store who decided what and when, separately from anything
   a computer can rebuild.
6. **Look at the failures.** Piles that mix subjects tell you what the method cannot see; write
   that down, as we do below.
7. **Record the model.** Name the model and its version so the result can be checked later.

## Known limits {#limits}

- Both distances compare *form*. Two subjects with the same outline (a tulip and a stylised tree)
  can share a pile; the reviewer separates them.
- Very small or very dense charts lose detail at 16 × 16 cells and in the image model.
- Some charts hold more than one figure; for now they are compared as one picture.
- The subject words are ours. They describe what the motif looks like today, not what it meant to
  the people who drew it centuries ago.

## Sources {#sources}

- Oquab, M. et al. (2023). [DINOv2: Learning Robust Visual Features without Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07193). arXiv:2304.07193.
- R Core Team. [`hclust`: Hierarchical Clustering](https://search.r-project.org/R/refmans/stats/html/hclust.html), R documentation.
- McInnes, L., Healy, J. and Astels, S. (2017). [hdbscan: Hierarchical density based clustering](https://joss.theoj.org/papers/10.21105/joss.00205). *Journal of Open Source Software* 2(11). An alternative we considered.
- Radford, A. et al. (2021). [Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020) (CLIP). Considered for naming suggestions; not used, because its guesses on small pattern charts are unreliable.
